lead: An inertial navigation system carries its own sensors and asks nothing of the outside world. Three accelerometers measure the push needed to hold a proof mass still, three gyros measure how fast the aircraft turns, and a computer integrates these to give velocity and position. Nothing is transmitted, so nothing can be jammed. The catch is drift: small sensor biases integrate into large position errors, so the answer is good for minutes and wanders over hours. INS flies airliners, missiles, submarines and spacecraft, usually blended with GPS (see 5.8).
prereq: You need 5.4 for gyro behaviour, 5.1 for the frames, and the accelerometer material in Unit 4.

sections.h3: Accelerometers measure specific force, gyros measure rate

blocks.text: An accelerometer holds a small proof mass. When the case accelerates the mass lags; a strain gauge, capacitor or piezoelectric crystal senses the displacement (Unit 4). A force-rebalance accelerometer pushes the mass back to null with a coil and outputs the coil current, keeping the sensor linear and stiff.

The output is specific force f, not acceleration in space. At rest the accelerometer reads 1 g upward: the ground pushes the mass up. In free fall it reads zero, though it accelerates at 9.81 m/s². To get inertial acceleration, add gravity back.

blocks.where: a is inertial acceleration (m/s²); f is measured specific force (m/s²); g is gravitational acceleration (m/s²), 9.81 m/s² downward. At rest f is 9.81 m/s² upward, so a = 0.

blocks.text: Gyros are rate sensors. A ring laser gyro sends two beams round a triangular cavity in opposite directions; rotation makes their path lengths differ, and the beat frequency is proportional to rate (the Sagnac effect). A fibre-optic gyro does the same in a coil of fibre with no moving parts. MEMS gyros shake a tiny mass and read the Coriolis force. Output is angular rate ω in °/s or °/h; one integration gives angle.

Bias is the output at zero input; scale factor error is the slope error, in ppm or %. Gyro bias is quoted in °/h and accelerometer bias in mg, where 1 mg = 0.00981 m/s² and 1 µg = 9.81 × 10⁻⁶ m/s² (one millionth of a g).

sections.h3: Frames, mechanizations and the inertial chain

blocks.text: Four frames matter. The inertial frame does not rotate. The Earth-fixed (ECEF) frame rotates with the Earth. The local navigation frame has north, east and down (NED) axes at the aircraft. The body frame is bolted to the airframe: x forward, y right, z down. Vectors move between frames by a direction cosine matrix (DCM, a 3×3 matrix of direction cosines), or by a quaternion — four numbers with no singularity at 90° pitch. Attitude is the DCM from body to NED.

Two mechanizations exist. In a gimballed system the sensors sit on a platform that torque motors hold level and pointing north while the aircraft turns around it, so the sensors see almost no rotation. In a strapdown system the sensors are bolted to the airframe and see the full rotation rate, so the computer carries attitude continuously. Strapdown won — smaller, cheaper, more reliable — at the cost of computing power and a wider sensor range.

items: Gyros give body rates ω; integrate them with the DCM to update body-to-NED attitude.
Accelerometers give f in body axes; rotate f into NED with that same DCM.
Add gravity: a = f + g, where g points down (third component +g in NED).
Integrate a once for velocity, then again for position.
Feed position back to the attitude step so the local level follows the Earth's curvature.

sections.h3: Alignment, Schuler tuning and error growth

blocks.text: Before use the INS must be aligned: its starting attitude must be found. Levelling uses the accelerometers — any tilt puts a horizontal component of gravity into f, so the pitch and roll that null it are correct. Gyrocompassing uses the gyros: the Earth turns at 15.04 °/h and its horizontal component points north. Rotating the heading until the sensed horizontal rate is zero finds north with no magnetic reference. Alignment needs a few minutes and the aircraft still.

A feedback from position to attitude is tuned to the Schuler period. A level platform carried over a round Earth behaves like a pendulum of length equal to the Earth's radius. Tuned to that natural period, a horizontal acceleration produces no steady tilt: the platform swings instead of drifting off level as the aircraft crosses the curved Earth.

blocks.where: T is the Schuler period (s); R = 6.371 × 10⁶ m is the Earth's radius; g = 9.81 m/s².

blocks.text: Errors after alignment grow by integration. An accelerometer bias b gives velocity error bt and position error ½bt². A gyro bias ε tilts the platform by εt, giving false horizontal acceleration gεt and position error gεt³/6. Gyro quality dominates: an accelerometer bias is painful, a gyro bias is fatal over hours.

blocks.where: Δp is position error (m); b is accelerometer bias (m/s²); ε is gyro bias (rad/s); t is time since alignment (s); g = 9.81 m/s².

blocks.text: With the Schuler loop closed, an accelerometer bias gives a bounded oscillating position error instead of ½bt². A gyro bias still gives a position error that grows steadily with time (a ramp with an 84.4 min ripple); only the tilt stays bounded, so gyro bias remains the dominant long-term error. The t² and t³ formulas above describe the unaided open-loop case. The cure is external aid — a satellite fix, or a Kalman filter blending the two (see 5.8).

figure.caption: The strapdown chain: sensor rates give attitude, attitude rotates specific force into the navigation frame, gravity is added, then two integrations give velocity and position. The dashed return is the Schuler loop.

examples.question: An inertial system is aligned on the ground and then runs unaided for 100 s. An accelerometer bias of 1 mg acts along a horizontal axis. (a) Find the velocity and position error at 100 s. (b) In a separate case, a gyro bias of 0.01 °/h runs for one hour; find the resulting velocity and position error. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
steps: Convert the accelerometer bias to SI: b = 1 mg = 1 × 10⁻³ × 9.81 = 9.81 × 10⁻³ m/s².
(b) Convert the gyro bias: ε = 0.01 °/h = 0.01 × 4.849 × 10⁻⁶ = 4.849 × 10⁻⁸ rad/s.
(b) The tilt grows as εt; at the end of the hour it is 4.849 × 10⁻⁸ × 3600 = 1.745 × 10⁻⁴ rad. This is the final tilt, not a constant tilt.
(b) Position error = gεt³/6 = 9.81 × 4.849 × 10⁻⁸ × 3600³ / 6 = 3.70 × 10³ m, about 3.7 km.
examples.answer: The 1 mg accelerometer bias gives 0.981 m/s and 49.05 m in 100 s; the 0.01 °/h gyro bias gives 3.08 m/s and about 3.7 km in one hour — the gyro error still dominates.
examples.check:
import math
b = 1e-3 * 9.81
t = 100.0
v1 = b * t
p1 = 0.5 * b * t**2
eps = math.radians(0.01) / 3600.0
T = 3600.0
v2 = 0.5 * 9.81 * eps * T**2
p2 = 9.81 * eps * T**3 / 6.0
print(round(v1, 3))
print(round(p1, 2))
print(round(v2, 3))
print(round(p2))

traps: An accelerometer at rest reads 1 g, not zero — it senses specific force. Writing a = f and forgetting gravity loses marks.
Velocity error from accelerometer bias is bt; position error is ½bt². Forgetting the ½ is the commonest slip.
Convert units first: 1 °/h = 4.849 × 10⁻⁶ rad/s, 1 mg = 0.00981 m/s².
Gimballed and strapdown are mechanizations, not sensor types; the same ring laser gyro can sit on a gimbal or be bolted down.
Gyrocompassing senses Earth's rotation of 15.04 °/h, not magnetic north, so magnetic variation never enters alignment.

quiz.q: What does an accelerometer in an INS actually measure?
quiz.a: Specific force — the non-gravitational push per unit mass. It reads 9.81 m/s² upward at rest and zero in free fall; add gravity back to get acceleration in space.

quiz.q: Why does a strapdown system demand more computation than a gimballed one?
quiz.a: Its sensors are bolted to the airframe and see the full rotation rate, so attitude must be integrated continuously in software. Gimbals stabilise physically, so the sensors see almost no rotation.

quiz.q: Why is the inertial loop tuned to the 84.4 min Schuler period?
quiz.a: So the platform behaves like a pendulum of length equal to the Earth's radius. A horizontal acceleration then causes no steady tilt; the platform oscillates about level instead of drifting off it as the aircraft crosses the curved Earth.

quiz.q: An accelerometer bias of 2 mg acts for 60 s. Find the velocity and position error. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
A gyro bias of 0.05 °/h is left uncorrected for 30 minutes. Find the position error using gεt³/6.
Why does a gyro bias give a position error growing as t³ while an accelerometer bias gives t²?
quiz.a: The gyro bias first tilts the platform by εt; the tilt turns gravity into a false horizontal acceleration gεt, which is integrated twice for position. A constant accelerometer bias is already an acceleration and needs only two integrations.

quiz.q: Gyrocompassing is easy near the equator and hard near the poles. Explain.
quiz.a: Ω = 15.04 °/h is the Earth's rotation rate and φ is the latitude, so the sensed horizontal Earth rate is Ω cos φ. This falls to zero at the pole while gyro bias stays fixed; the signal-to-noise ratio collapses, so alignment takes longer and eventually fails.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern airliners fly strapdown units on fibre-optic or MEMS gyros, and the same chips sit in phones. Cold-atom interferometers promise biases below 10⁻⁴ °/h with no gimbals. Transfer alignment — aligning a missile's INS from its carrier before release — is a lively design problem. Search 'ring laser gyro dither', 'Sagnac effect fibre gyro' and 'transfer alignment'.
